Space Age Lodge sign, Gila Bend

The roadside sign of a 1960s desert motel: a tilted flying-saucer disc with the lodge’s name in blue capitals around its rim, under a later chain-hotel panel.

Source
Library of Congress: John Margolies, Space Age Lodge sign, Gila Bend, Arizona, 2003
Creator
Al Stovall (owner and developer, per Roadside America)
Made
Motel opened 1963 or 1965, sources differ; photographed 2003
Style
Googie (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Roadside, futuristic, playful
Evidence
Downloaded and inspected John Margolies’s 2003 color slide, Library of Congress LC-MA05-1423, 704 × 1024 px, in a scratchpad. Not stored.
Reviewed
2 October 2026
Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

Roadside America reports that Al Stovall built the lodge and that his plastics factory made its space-age decorations. It gives the opening as 1963 in one account and 1965 in another (from the restaurant menu), and says three satellite replicas on the roof were replaced by a flying saucer in a 1969 renovation. Roadside America.

The Library of Congress record gives only the title and the date of the photograph. Library of Congress.

Observed

  • A large disc, tilted up to the right, shows a flying saucer from below: a pale dome ringed with red portholes, gray radiating panels, and a rim of small bulbs.
  • “SPACE AGE LODGE” runs around the lower rim of the disc in heavy blue capitals that follow the curve.
  • Above it, a separate shield-shaped Best Western panel in navy and gold carries “SPACE AGE LODGE” in white serif capitals; this is later chain branding.
  • Below, rectangular reader boards list rooms, cable TV, a coffee shop, and a salad bar in black and red capitals.
  • At left, the lobby has a domed cylinder on top and a blue steel space frame with slanted struts.
  • The ground is an even, deep blue desert sky.

Why it belongs

The tilted disc is a Googie habit: the sign is not a rectangle but a symbol of the future, set at an angle so it seems to fly.

The serif chain panel above shows how later branding sits on top of the original sign without its energy.

Borrow

Set a name around the curve of a disc or ellipse, and tilt the whole badge a few degrees.

Edge a badge with a row of small dots, like sign bulbs.
